merge_rule: 2-of-3 promotion: a chapter is 'hard' only if >= 2 reviewers flagged it hard. Otherwise soft if >= 1 reviewer flagged it.

reasons: Round 1 flagged for reading as API documentation. Round 2 re-reading confirms restructuring is present but chapter still spends disproportionate space on GrowthBook internals that dilute the central architectural argument
The divergences section names the operator-vs-agent split but does not prescribe a concrete solution pattern for closing the loop
Edge-case section has grown with operational details (formatCost precision, getAllGrowthBookFeatures, etc.) that dilute the chapter's focus
merged_flags.suggested_angle: Cut GrowthBook operational details to a single paragraph. Expand divergences with a concrete in-process metrics bus interface pattern showing what the API would look like and what call sites would change.

reasons: Thorough cataloging of all 17 failure modes but the many-to-many mapping means the reader cannot quickly see which modes have the deepest defenses and which are most exposed

Failure modes 6.2, 6.4, 6.10, 6.17 are all 'prompt-level, no structural mechanism' but the chapter does not explain WHY cc chose prompt-level over structural enforcement -- deliberate tradeoff or oversight?
Token budget code snippets for 6.7 are duplicated from Chapter 10 without adding new analytical depth specific to the failure-mode framing
merged_flags.suggested_angle: Add a severity-exposure matrix at the start showing defense depth (structural/prompt/none) vs exploitability (easy/hard/theoretical). For each prompt-level-only defense, add a one-sentence design rationale explaining why structural enforcement was not chosen.

reasons: Reads as a feature walkthrough rather than architectural analysis -- describes WHAT each subsystem does without extracting the deeper pattern about why cc's observability is post-hoc rather than real-time
The dual-identity observation (ant vs external debug logging) is mentioned but its architectural implications for production incident diagnosis are not explored
HER cross-reference to Section 6.6 (silent failures) is token -- does not explain how debug log format could enable automated silent-failure detection
merged_flags.suggested_angle: Restructure around the post-hoc vs real-time observability spectrum. Show where cc sits (firmly post-hoc), what architectural constraints prevent real-time self-monitoring, and what a reader would need to add for real-time failure detection.

reasons: ETH Zurich finding that context files reduce task success while increasing cost is mentioned in overview but not carried through as a design constraint for the rest of the chapter
Closed four-type taxonomy (user/feedback/project/reference) presented without explaining why these four specifically or what happens when content does not fit
Side-query relevance evaluation adds latency and cost to every query but the chapter does not quantify this overhead or discuss the tradeoff
merged_flags.suggested_angle: Add a section on the cost-benefit tension: explain how cc's 200-line cap and type exclusions respond to the ETH Zurich finding, and quantify side-query overhead so readers can assess whether the tiered approach is worth it.

reasons: Missing 'Where cc diverges from the published pattern' section -- no analysis of how cc's hook implementation differs from HER Pattern 12 (Deterministic Lifecycle Hooks)
Five hook types enumerated without explaining why these five specifically or what security implications each type carries, particularly agent and function types that execute arbitrary code
HER cross-reference limited to Pattern 12 and Configuration Surfaces -- no connection to broader failure-mode defenses or the permission system
merged_flags.suggested_angle: Add a divergences section analyzing exit-code semantics, SSRF guard on HTTP hooks, and supply-chain risk of function hooks. Connect hooks to the permission pipeline and explain why hooks are NOT the final arbiter for safety-critical paths.
